bracket: [Textbook misprint: the question as printed reads "vander Waals focres". Two defects in one phrase — the name is set as a single word where it is "van der Waals", and "focres" is a transposition of "forces". Transcribed as printed; neither affects the answer, which is physical adsorption (physisorption).]

[Textbook note (not an error): the exercise asks this same question twice. It appears here as item 4 A, "A finely divided substance is more effective as adsorbent", and again as item 3 H, "Explain why finely divided substance is more effective as adsorbent?". Both are answered on the same ground — adsorption is a surface phenomenon, so a larger surface area for a given mass means greater adsorption.]

[Textbook misprint: section 11.2.3 of the chapter, which is the passage a student would turn to for the examples this question asks for, is headed "Examples of Absorption" but is mostly about ADSORPTION. It opens with one genuine absorption example (cotton dipped in water), then continues "Some more examples of adsorption :" and lists three adsorption examples — gases on finely divided metals, gases on activated charcoal, and the removal of an organic dye by charcoal. Those three are examples of adsorption, not of absorption, so the heading does not describe the section. The distinction itself is set out correctly in Table 11.1.]
